questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

(i) Taxonomy.

(ii) Binomial nomenclature. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Taxonomy** is the branch of biology that **identifies, names and classifies organisms into groups (taxa)** according to their similarities and their evolutionary relationships. The groups form a hierarchy: kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species.

**(ii) Binomial nomenclature** is the **internationally accepted system of giving every species a two-word Latin name**, introduced by **Carolus Linnaeus**. The **first word is the genus** (it starts with a capital letter) and the **second word is the species** (all in small letters); the name is printed in *italics* or underlined when handwritten, e.g. *Homo sapiens* (man), *Zea mays* (maize), *Theobroma cacao* (cocoa).

The system is useful because a species has **one name recognised in every country and language**, which avoids the confusion caused by common (local) names, and the genus name shows which species are closely related.

questions.enonce_markdown: Explain why viruses are not considered as cellular organisms. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
A **cellular organism** is built of one or more cells, each with a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material, and it carries out all the characteristics of life by itself. Viruses are **acellular** for these reasons:

1. **No cell structure:** a virus is only a core of **nucleic acid** (DNA *or* RNA, never both) surrounded by a **protein coat (capsid)** made of capsomeres, sometimes with an outer lipid envelope. It has **no plasma membrane, no cytoplasm, no nucleus and no organelles**.
2. **No ribosomes or enzymes of its own** for protein synthesis and no ATP-producing system: it does **not respire, feed, grow, excrete or respond** to stimuli on its own, so it is metabolically inert outside a host.
3. **It can reproduce only inside a living host cell**, using the host's ribosomes, enzymes, amino acids and ATP to make new virus particles (an **obligate intracellular parasite**). It does not divide by mitosis or binary fission.
4. **Outside the host it behaves like a non-living particle:** some viruses can be **crystallised** and stored for years, and become active again when they enter a host.
5. It is **extremely small** (about 20 to 300 nm, far below the size of the smallest cell) and is visible only with an electron microscope.

For these reasons viruses are usually placed outside the five kingdoms.

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe the life cycle of a named retrovirus. *[10 marks]* *(5, 5, 10 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Named retrovirus: the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).**

**Structure.** HIV has two identical single-stranded **RNA** molecules and the enzymes **reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease** inside a protein capsid, surrounded by an **envelope** taken from the host membrane that carries the glycoprotein **gp120/gp41**. The host cells are the **CD4 (helper T) lymphocytes**, and also macrophages.

**Life cycle (in order):**

1. **Attachment:** gp120 binds to the **CD4 receptor** (and a co-receptor, CCR5 or CXCR4) on the host cell.
2. **Entry and uncoating:** gp41 makes the viral envelope **fuse with the plasma membrane**; the capsid enters the cytoplasm and **breaks down**, releasing the RNA and enzymes.
3. **Reverse transcription:** **reverse transcriptase** makes a **single-stranded DNA copy (cDNA)** from the viral RNA template, breaks down the RNA, then makes the complementary strand to form **double-stranded viral DNA**.
4. **Integration:** the viral DNA enters the **nucleus** and **integrase** inserts it into a host chromosome, where it is a **provirus**. It may stay **latent** for years, copied with the host DNA at each cell division.
5. **Transcription:** when the cell is activated, host **RNA polymerase** transcribes the provirus into **viral mRNA** and new genomic RNA.
6. **Translation:** host **ribosomes** make the viral proteins (capsid proteins, enzymes, envelope glycoproteins); **protease** cuts the long polyprotein into functional proteins.
7. **Assembly:** new capsids form around two copies of RNA and the enzymes, close to the plasma membrane, which now carries viral glycoproteins.
8. **Budding and release:** the new virus particles **bud off** and take part of the host membrane as their **envelope**; they mature and go on to infect other CD4 cells.

The host cells are finally destroyed (and the number of CD4 cells falls), which weakens immunity and leads to **AIDS**.

*Diagram expected:* a cycle with arrows labelled: attachment, fusion, uncoating, reverse transcription (RNA to DNA), integration into the host chromosome, transcription, translation, assembly, budding.
